newsitem.title: GERMANY: German builders too dear for Transrapid railway.
newsitem.headline: German builders too dear for Transrapid railway.

text.p: Germany's Transrapid high-speed railway will search for cheaper, foreign construction groups after parting company with the three German firms orginally intended to build it.

Transport Minister Matthias Wissmann, the official leading public involvement in the near 10 billion mark ($5.8 billion) venture, said on Friday it was now clear that the Transrapid could only be built at the right price with a fully open, international tender.
"For this kind of project, without a real tender and real bidding you do not get the competition and the cost reduction you need," he said after a news briefing in Bonn.
Wissmann cast doubt on media reports earlier in the day suggesting that the three firms -- Philipp Holzmann, Hochtief and Bilfinger+Berger -- had decided to walk out of the project.
"It's question of whether they decided to leave or whether the consortium decided not to take them," Wissmann said.

It was earlier confirmed that steel and engineering group Thyssen, engineering giant Siemens and the Deutsche Bahn railways operating company would proceed with the project, under Deutsche Bahn's leadership.
They are now negotiating with potential foreign investors and want to add another European partner.
The construction groups, while not commenting on whether they had plans to enter the open tender process, made clear that cost was the issue on which their participation had foundered.
"We are not ready to participate in Transrapid at any price," a Hochtief spokeswoman said from the group's headquarters in Essen in response to enquiries.
A month ago Hochtief chairman Hans-Peter Keitel listed Transrapid as one of the projects that it saw as most attractive in terms of its plans for greater cooperation with Holzmann.

German construction groups are often criticised as too expensive and have difficulty competing with foreign companies, which frequently use workers who do not receive the full range of German social and work benefits.

Transrapid, which is due to come into operation between Hamburg and Berlin by 2005, is expected to entail construction costs of more than six billion marks and employ around 18,000 building workers from 1998.
The German government is due to cover the costs of building the track itself.
Wissmann did not specify the extent of the price cut he expected by opening up the project to competing bidders, nor which companies he thought would come forward.

But building sector analysts said the kind of profit margin available for a project like Transrapid was never likely to be attractive and most welcomed the departure of construction groups from the venture.

"Transrapid is very much a prestige object and as such factors often come into play that are not purely commercial," said Karin Brinkmann, an analyst at Munich-based Bayerische Hypotheken und Wechselbank.
She added that she would not be too enthusiastic if any of the German groups decided to re-enter the bidding separately.
The Frankfurt-listed shares in the three builders initially rose on the Transrapid news but later fell back as analysts said it did not make for any change in value of the stocks.
